question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.
I had seen / her with her mother / in the cinema hall / yesterday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. I had seen.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the Past Perfect Tense ("I had seen"), but there is only a single action described, with no second past action to serve as a reference point.

• Rule — Past Perfect Tense: The Past Perfect ("had + V3") is used only when two actions occurred in the past, to show which one happened first (the earlier action takes "had + V3", the later one takes Simple Past). Since the sentence mentions only one past action (seeing her at the cinema "yesterday"), the Simple Past Tense "I saw" should be used instead of "I had seen".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in the cinema hall" is correct as printed; it is simply a prepositional phrase of place and carries no error.

• Option 2: "her with her mother" is correct as printed; the object and accompanying phrase are correctly formed.

• Option 3: "yesterday" is correct as printed; it is a simple adverb of time and needs no correction.

NOTE

• A time marker like "yesterday" signals the Simple Past Tense, not the Past Perfect — whenever such a marker of a single completed past action is present without any second, earlier action, avoid "had + V3".

• Commonly tested error type: using Past Perfect where Simple Past is required, and vice versa, is one of the most frequent "spot the error" traps in SSC exams.

question:
Select the option to replace the incorrect word in the following sentence.
Chotu is a bright young child, who yearn to go to school but works in his uncle’s dhaba.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. yearns.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The relative pronoun "who" in this sentence refers back to its antecedent "child", which is third person singular.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: When a relative pronoun ("who/which/that") is the subject of a relative clause, the verb in that clause must agree in number and person with the relative pronoun's antecedent, not with the pronoun itself. Since "child" is singular, the verb must take the singular present-tense form "yearns" (V1 + s/es), not the base form "yearn".

• Applying the rule: "who yearn" must be corrected to "who yearns", matching the parallel singular verb already used later in the sentence — "works".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "worked" is incorrect; changing the tense to past does not fix the subject-verb disagreement, and it also breaks the Present tense already established by "works" later in the sentence.

• Option 2: "working" is incorrect; the present participle cannot function alone as the main verb of the relative clause without an auxiliary ("is working").

• Option 4: "yearned" is incorrect for the same reason as Option 1 — it wrongly shifts the sentence into the past tense.

NOTE

• Singular antecedents commonly missed in SSC exams: each, everyone, either, neither, child, one of the + plural noun — all take a singular verb.

• Always identify the true antecedent of "who/which/that" before deciding the verb form; do not simply match the verb to the nearest noun.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
He _________ a long distance
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. ran.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence **"He _________ a long distance" requires a finite main verb in the Simple Past Tense, since the action of running is being reported as a completed, single event with the subject "He"** directly followed by the verb and object.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense: Subject + V2 (past form) + Object. The past form of the irregular verb "run" is "ran".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "runned" is incorrect; "run" is an irregular verb, so its past form is "ran", not the regularly-formed "runned".

• Option 2: "running" is incorrect; the present participle "running" cannot serve as the main finite verb of the sentence without an auxiliary verb (e.g., "was running").

• Option 4: "run" is incorrect as a finite past-tense verb here; "run" is the base form (V1) and, though identical to the past participle (V3), it cannot stand alone as a Simple Past verb.

NOTE

• Common irregular verbs with the same trap: run–ran–run, swim–swam–swum, ring–rang–rung, drink–drank–drunk — the base form (V1) and past participle (V3) look identical to each other in some of these, but the Simple Past (V2) is distinct.

• Always check whether the sentence needs a finite verb (a complete, tensed verb) or a non-finite form (participle/infinitive) before choosing an option.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into three segments. One of them may contain an adverbial usage error. Select the option that has the segment with the error. If you don’t find any error, select ‘No error’ as your answer.
Mr. Narayanan / is a rather / lazy man.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Mr. Narayanan is a rather lazy man" uses the adverb "rather" correctly, placed immediately before the adjective "lazy", which it modifies.

• Rule — Position of "rather": The intensifying adverb "rather" is normally placed directly before the adjective or adverb it modifies (e.g., "rather + adjective + noun"), as in "a rather lazy man", "a rather difficult task". This is exactly the pattern used in the given sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Mr. Narayanan" is correct as printed; it is simply the subject of the sentence and carries no error.

• Option 3: "is a rather" is correct as printed; the linking verb "is", the article "a", and the adverb "rather" are all correctly placed before the adjective that follows.

• Option 4: "lazy man." is correct as printed; the adjective "lazy" correctly modifies the noun "man", and "rather" in the preceding segment correctly intensifies "lazy".

NOTE

• With "a"/"an" + adjective + noun, "rather" can appear either before the article ("rather a lazy man") or after it ("a rather lazy man") — both are grammatically acceptable in English, though "a rather lazy man" is the more common order.

• Do not confuse "rather" (an intensifier) with "rather than" (a comparative conjunction meaning "instead of") — the two have entirely different grammatical functions.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Trees are (1)________ best gift of nature for us. They make the environment beautiful and clean. Water and sunlight are very important to helping trees grow. Human beings get food from trees. Trees also give us wood and shade. Houses, chairs, and toys (2)________ from wood we receive from trees. Trees can be called the best friends of mankind. Many animals get their food from leaves, vegetables, and fruits grown (3)________ trees. They also live in the shadows of trees. We (4)________ cutting trees to save nature. Children and adults need to plant more trees and teach each other to stop causing harm to (5)________. One tree can save many lives.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. the.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank comes before the superlative adjective "best", in the phrase **"Trees are ________ best gift of nature for us."**

• Rule — Article with Superlatives: The definite article "the" is always used before a superlative degree adjective (best, tallest, most beautiful, etc.), because a superlative singles out one specific item from a group, making it definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "a" is incorrect; the indefinite article "a" is used with non-specific singular nouns, not with superlative adjectives.

• Option 3: "an" is incorrect for the same reason as "a", and additionally "best" begins with a consonant sound, so "an" would be wrong even before a non-superlative noun.

• Option 4: "No article" is incorrect; omitting the article before a superlative adjective is ungrammatical in standard English.

NOTE

• Other common "the + superlative" SSC patterns: the most important, the tallest, the least expensive, the highest.

• Exception to note: "the" is dropped before a superlative used as an adverb without a following noun (e.g., "He runs fastest"), but this does not apply when the superlative directly precedes a noun, as here.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Trees are (1)________ best gift of nature for us. They make the environment beautiful and clean. Water and sunlight are very important to helping trees grow. Human beings get food from trees. Trees also give us wood and shade. Houses, chairs, and toys (2)________ from wood we receive from trees. Trees can be called the best friends of mankind. Many animals get their food from leaves, vegetables, and fruits grown (3)________ trees. They also live in the shadows of trees. We (4)________ cutting trees to save nature. Children and adults need to plant more trees and teach each other to stop causing harm to (5)________. One tree can save many lives.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. are made.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject "Houses, chairs, and toys" is plural, and the action of being manufactured "from wood" is a general, ongoing fact, requiring the Simple Present Passive.

• Rule — Simple Present Passive: Subject (plural) + are + V3 (past participle). Since "make" is an irregular verb, its past participle is "made", giving the correct passive form "are made".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "had make" is incorrect; "had" is a Past Perfect auxiliary and must be followed by a past participle ("had made"), not the base form "make", and the tense itself does not fit the passage's general present-tense description.

• Option 3: "was make" is incorrect; "was" is a singular past-tense auxiliary, which does not agree with the plural subject, and it must also be followed by a past participle ("was made"), not "make".

• Option 4: "will made" is incorrect; the future auxiliary "will" must be followed by the base form of the verb ("will make"), never by the past participle "made".

NOTE

• Passive voice formula to remember: be (am/is/are/was/were/will be) + V3. The auxiliary changes with tense and number, but the main verb always stays in its past participle (V3) form.

• Common irregular V3 forms tested in SSC cloze/passive questions: make–made, write–written, break–broken, take–taken, give–given.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Trees are (1)________ best gift of nature for us. They make the environment beautiful and clean. Water and sunlight are very important to helping trees grow. Human beings get food from trees. Trees also give us wood and shade. Houses, chairs, and toys (2)________ from wood we receive from trees. Trees can be called the best friends of mankind. Many animals get their food from leaves, vegetables, and fruits grown (3)________ trees. They also live in the shadows of trees. We (4)________ cutting trees to save nature. Children and adults need to plant more trees and teach each other to stop causing harm to (5)________. One tree can save many lives.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. on.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in the phrase **"fruits grown ________ trees"**, describing where fruits grow.

• Rule — Preposition of Position: The preposition "on" is used to show something growing or resting upon a surface or a plant/tree (e.g., "fruit grows on a tree", "leaves grow on branches").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "out" is incorrect; "out" indicates movement away from an enclosed space and does not fit the sense of fruit growing on a tree.

• Option 3: "of" is incorrect; "of" shows possession or composition, not physical location on a surface.

• Option 4: "for" is incorrect; "for" indicates purpose or beneficiary, which does not fit the meaning required here.

NOTE

• Common preposition pairs tested in SSC cloze passages: grow on (a tree), live in (a house/forest), depend on, arrive at/in, married to.

• Do not confuse "grow on" (physical location) with "grow up" (to mature), which has an entirely different meaning.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Trees are (1)________ best gift of nature for us. They make the environment beautiful and clean. Water and sunlight are very important to helping trees grow. Human beings get food from trees. Trees also give us wood and shade. Houses, chairs, and toys (2)________ from wood we receive from trees. Trees can be called the best friends of mankind. Many animals get their food from leaves, vegetables, and fruits grown (3)________ trees. They also live in the shadows of trees. We (4)________ cutting trees to save nature. Children and adults need to plant more trees and teach each other to stop causing harm to (5)________. One tree can save many lives.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. should stop.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in **"We ________ cutting trees to save nature"**, expressing moral obligation or advice.

• Rule — Modal Verbs: A modal verb (can, may, should, must, will, etc.) is always followed directly by the base form (V1) of the main verb, with no "-ed", "-s", or "to" attached. "Should" is the modal that correctly expresses advice/obligation ("we should stop") in this context.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "can stopped" is incorrect; the modal "can" must be followed by the base form "stop", not the past form "stopped".

• Option 2: "may stopped" is incorrect for the same reason; "may" must be followed by the base form "stop".

• Option 4: "have stop" is incorrect; "have" as a Present Perfect auxiliary must be followed by a past participle ("have stopped"), not the base form "stop", and it does not fit the intended sense of advice here either.

NOTE

• Rule to remember: Modal + V1 (base form only) — never add "-s", "-ed", "-ing", or "to" after a modal verb (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must).

• "Should" is the standard modal for expressing advice, duty, or recommendation in SSC grammar questions.

question:
Comprehension: In the following passage some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Trees are (1)________ best gift of nature for us. They make the environment beautiful and clean. Water and sunlight are very important to helping trees grow. Human beings get food from trees. Trees also give us wood and shade. Houses, chairs, and toys (2)________ from wood we receive from trees. Trees can be called the best friends of mankind. Many animals get their food from leaves, vegetables, and fruits grown (3)________ trees. They also live in the shadows of trees. We (4)________ cutting trees to save nature. Children and adults need to plant more trees and teach each other to stop causing harm to (5)________. One tree can save many lives.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. nature.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in **"stop causing harm to ________", where the preposition "to" must be followed by a noun** (the object of the preposition).

• Rule — Preposition + Noun: A preposition is always followed by a noun, pronoun, or gerund, never by a plain adjective. "Nature" is the noun form that correctly completes the phrase "harm to nature", matching the passage's overall theme of trees and the environment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "nurturing" is incorrect; it is the gerund/present participle form of the verb "nurture" and does not fit the required noun meaning ("harm to the environment"), producing an illogical sense.

• Option 3: "nurture" is incorrect; used here it would function as a verb, not a noun object of the preposition "to", and grammatically cannot follow "to" (the preposition) as a plain object without a change in meaning.

• Option 4: "natural" is incorrect; it is an adjective and cannot serve as the object of the preposition "to", which requires a noun.

NOTE

• Distinguish the related word family: nature (noun) — natural (adjective) — nurture (verb/noun) — nurturing (adjective/gerund) — a very common SSC vocabulary-cum-grammar trap.

• Always check the part of speech required by the sentence structure (here, a noun after a preposition) before choosing between similar-looking word forms.

question:
Select the most appropriate to fill in the blank.
The boxer was knocked out cold by a powerful________ punch to the jaw.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. right.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The words "write", "wright", "rite", and "right" are homophones — they sound identical but differ in spelling and meaning.

• Here, the blank describes the punch as being thrown with the right hand (a "right punch" is a standard boxing term for a punch delivered with the right fist), so the correct word is the adjective "right".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "write" is incorrect; it is a verb meaning to form letters/words on a surface, and makes no sense describing a punch.

• Option 2: "wright" is incorrect; it is a noun (often used in compounds like "playwright" or "wheelwright") meaning a maker or builder, unrelated to boxing.

• Option 3: "rite" is incorrect; it means a religious or ceremonial act (e.g., "a rite of passage"), which does not fit the sentence.

NOTE

• Commonly confused homophone sets tested in SSC exams: write/right/rite/wright, there/their/they're, principal/principle, stationary/stationery, board/bored.

• In boxing terminology, punches are commonly identified by the hand thrown — a "right" or a "left".

question:
Select the option that can substitute the bracketed word segment meaningfully.
If you behave well and exhibit good manners, then (people will be likely to remember you) in a positive way.
option_4: people are likely to remember you
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. people are likely to remember you.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed segment "people will be likely to remember you" contains a double/redundant modal-like structure — combining "will be" with "likely to", which is grammatically faulty.

• Rule — "be likely to" construction: The correct structure is Subject + am/is/are + likely to + base verb, used to express probability (e.g., "It is likely to rain", "She is likely to win"). The future auxiliary "will" should not be combined with "be likely to" in this way.

• Applying the rule: "people will be likely to remember you" is corrected to "people are likely to remember you", using the plural present-tense auxiliary "are" that agrees with the plural subject "people".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "people likely you remember" is incorrect; the word order is scrambled and the sentence is not grammatically coherent.

• Option 2: "people are like remember you" is incorrect; "like" cannot substitute for "likely" here, and "remember" cannot directly follow it without "to".

• Option 3: "people will like in remember" is incorrect; this word order and the preposition "in" before "remember" produce an ungrammatical sentence.

NOTE

• "Likely" is an adjective and must be followed by "to + base verb" (e.g., "likely to happen", "likely to succeed"), not by "will" or a bare verb.

• Do not confuse "likely" (adjective, probability) with "like" (verb: to enjoy, or preposition: similar to).

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute the underlined word segment in the given sentence.
Delivering that furniture to the tenth floor without the lift and an incline is incredibly foolish and next to impossible .
option_1: like a tree known by its fruits
option_2: like nailing jelly to the tree
option_3: as tight as the bark of the tree
option_4: like going between the bark and the tree
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. like nailing jelly to the tree.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "like nailing jelly to a/the tree" means an extremely difficult or virtually impossible task to accomplish, since jelly cannot be pinned down with a nail. (व्यावहारिक रूप से असंभव कार्य)
◦ Example: Getting the whole committee to agree on one date is like nailing jelly to the tree.

• This matches the underlined phrase "incredibly foolish and next to impossible", which describes an impractical, almost unachievable task — carrying furniture up ten floors without a lift.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "like a tree known by its fruits" (कर्म से पहचान) means a person is judged by the results of their actions, not by their words — unrelated to difficulty or foolishness.

• Option 3: "as tight as the bark of the tree" is not a standard English idiom with a recognized meaning matching the sentence; it does not express impossibility.

• Option 4: "like going between the bark and the tree" is a distorted form of the idiom "to come between the bark and the tree" (to interfere in others' private/family matters) — unrelated to the sense of an impossible task.

NOTE

• Other idioms expressing "impossible/very difficult" often asked in SSC: "a Herculean task", "a tall order", "to move heaven and earth", "easier said than done".

• Be careful not to confuse idioms that merely share a keyword (like "tree" or "bark" here) — always match the full meaning, not just the vocabulary.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
This makes readers contemplate the motives people have for performing acts of charity.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. overlook.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "contemplate" means to think about something deeply and carefully; to consider thoughtfully. (गहराई से विचार करना)

• Its antonym, "overlook", means to fail to notice or consider something; to not pay attention to it. (नज़रअंदाज़ करना) This is the direct opposite of deeply thinking something over.
◦ Example: Instead of contemplating the risks, he chose to overlook them entirely.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "understate" (कम करके बताना) means to describe something as smaller or less important than it really is — a different concept from thinking deeply, not a true opposite.

• Option 2: "follow up" means to pursue or continue with something further — this is unrelated to the act of thinking/not thinking about something.

• Option 4: "deviate" (भटकना) means to turn away from a course or standard — unrelated in meaning to "contemplate" or its opposite.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "contemplate": ponder, deliberate, reflect, mull over, meditate.

• Other antonym pairs of "consider/think about" often tested in SSC: heed × ignore, notice × overlook, ponder × disregard.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a spelling error.
In all instances of frustrasion, / you will always find / the anger directed towards / a single person only.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. In all instances of frustrasion.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "frustrasion" is misspelt in this segment; the correct spelling is "frustration" — a noun meaning a feeling of dissatisfaction arising from unresolved problems or unmet needs.
◦ Example: She could not hide her frustration at the delayed train.

• Spelling key: FRUS + TRA + TION. The ending is "-tion" (as in "action", "nation", "station"), not "-sion"; "frustrasion" wrongly substitutes "s" for the "t" before the suffix.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the anger directed towards" is correctly spelt as printed; it carries no error.

• Option 3: "you will always find" is correctly spelt as printed; it carries no error.

• Option 4: "a single person only" is correctly spelt as printed; it carries no error.

NOTE

• Common "-tion" vs "-sion" confusion in SSC spelling questions: words derived from verbs ending in "-te" usually take "-tion" (frustrate → frustration, educate → education), while words derived from verbs ending in "-d" or "-de" often take "-sion" (decide → decision, expand → expansion).

• Other frequently misspelt words of this type: occasion, possession, permission, admission, extension.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The movie ‘Desperate Ghosts’ was watched by my younger brother and he was _____________ horror.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. filled with.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase **"filled ________ horror" requires the correct preposition that collocates with the adjective "filled"** when describing an emotion.

• Rule — Fixed Preposition: The adjective "filled" is conventionally followed by the preposition "with" when indicating the emotion or substance that fills someone/something (e.g., "filled with joy", "filled with fear", "filled with horror").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "filled of" is incorrect; "of" is not the preposition that collocates with "filled" in this sense.

• Option 3: "filled on" is incorrect; "on" indicates position/surface and does not fit this fixed expression.

• Option 4: "filled off" is incorrect; "off" indicates separation or removal, which is contrary to the intended meaning of being full of an emotion.

NOTE

• Other fixed "adjective + preposition" combinations frequently tested in SSC: afraid of, fond of, married to, angry with (a person)/at (a thing), interested in, proud of.

• "Filled with" and "full of" are near-synonymous fixed expressions, both taking the preposition that follows their respective adjective/participle form.

question:
Read the sentence carefully and select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined part.
The sudden declaration of war between two countries led to a disarray.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. disorderly situation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "disarray" means a state of disorganization or untidiness; confusion. (अव्यवस्था, गड़बड़ी)
◦ Example: The sudden resignation of the CEO threw the company into disarray.

• "Disorderly situation" correctly captures this meaning of a chaotic, confused state, matching the context of a sudden declaration of war.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "peaceful treaty" (शांति संधि) means an agreement establishing peace — this is nearly the opposite of the confusion implied by "disarray".

• Option 3: "refined argument" means a polished, well-reasoned point of debate — unrelated to disorder or confusion.

• Option 4: "elusive situation" (मायावी/समझ से परे स्थिति) means a situation that is hard to grasp, understand, or pin down — this describes difficulty of understanding, not disorder, and so does not match "disarray".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "disarray": chaos, confusion, disorder, turmoil, mayhem.

• Antonym of "disarray": order, arrangement, organization — useful to know for antonym-based questions on the same word.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Conscientous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Conscientious" — an adjective meaning careful, diligent, and guided by a strong sense of what is right.
◦ Example: She is a conscientious worker who never misses a deadline.

• The printed option "Conscientous" is missing the "i" before the ending "-ous"; the correct ending is "-tious" (as in "conscientious"), not "-tous".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Acknowledgment" is correctly spelt; it is the standard (chiefly American) spelling, alongside the British variant "acknowledgement" — both are accepted as correct.

• Option 2: "Apparent" is correctly spelt as printed — meaning clearly visible or seemingly true.

• Option 3: "Fulfil" is correctly spelt as printed — the standard British spelling (American English also accepts "fulfill").

NOTE

• Spelling tip: words ending in the sound "-shuss" are often spelt "-tious" (conscientious, ambitious, cautious) or "-cious" (delicious, gracious, malicious) rather than "-tous" or "-cous".

• Other commonly misspelt SSC words in this family: ambiguous, courteous, righteous, spontaneous.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.
This gun should be handled with care and ____________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. kept at arm’s length.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to keep something/someone at arm’s length" means to avoid close contact with something or someone; to treat with caution and maintain a safe distance. (सुरक्षित दूरी बनाए रखना)
◦ Example: Given how dangerous the chemical is, it should always be kept at arm’s length.

• In the given sentence, a gun — being a dangerous object — logically fits the idea of being handled carefully and kept at a cautious distance, matching "handled with care and kept at arm’s length."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "nip in the bud" (शुरूआत में ही समाप्त करना) means to stop a problem at an early stage before it develops — unrelated to handling a physical object with caution.

• Option 2: "shot for safety" is not a recognized English idiom and does not fit the sentence.

• Option 3: "mince the matters" is a distortion of the idiom "to mince matters" (to speak diplomatically, usually used as "not mince matters" = to speak bluntly) — this does not fit the context of handling a gun with care.

NOTE

• Other idioms of caution/distance often tested in SSC: "to give a wide berth to", "to handle with kid gloves", "to tread carefully".

• Do not confuse "mince matters" (to speak) with idioms about physical caution — the two idiom families are often mixed up as distractors.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the word ‘echoed’ to fill in the blank.
The thunderous applause _________ through the stadium.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. reverberated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "echoed" means resounded; repeated or reflected sound that carried through a space. (गूंजना)

• "Reverberated" means to resound or re-echo, as sound repeatedly reflecting off surfaces, which is a close synonym of "echoed", matching the sense of applause resounding through a stadium.
◦ Example: The singer's voice reverberated through the concert hall.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "recoiled" (पीछे हटना) means to spring or jump back in alarm or disgust — this describes a physical/emotional reaction, not sound spreading through a space.

• Option 3: "bounced" means to spring back after hitting a surface — used for physical objects, not typically for the specific sense of sound "echoing" through a large space.

• Option 4: "pulsed" means to beat or throb rhythmically — describes a rhythmic pattern, not the resounding/echoing quality meant by "echoed".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "echo/echoed": resound, resonate, ring out.

• "Reverberate" is frequently tested in SSC vocabulary questions in contexts of sound (in a hall, stadium, valley) as well as figuratively (an idea "reverberating" through society).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Chaste
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Pure.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Chaste" means pure, virtuous, and morally clean, especially in conduct or speech; free from impurity. (शुद्ध, पवित्र)
◦ Example: She led a chaste and simple life devoted to prayer.

• "Pure" carries the same core meaning of moral cleanliness and freedom from corruption, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Flashy" (भड़कीला) means showy or gaudy in a vulgar way — nearly the opposite of the modest, restrained sense of "chaste".

• Option 2: "Corrupt" (भ्रष्ट) means dishonest or morally depraved — a direct antonym of "chaste", not a synonym.

• Option 3: "Sullied" (दागदार) means stained or defiled — also an antonym, describing the loss of purity rather than purity itself.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "chaste": virtuous, pure, modest, virginal, decent.

• Antonyms of "chaste": corrupt, impure, immoral, sullied — useful to recognize since these often appear as distractors in synonym questions, as seen with Options 2 and 3 here.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Cheerful
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Gloomy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Cheerful" means noticeably happy and optimistic; full of good spirits. (प्रसन्नचित्त)

• "Gloomy" means dark, dismal, or feeling sad and without hope, which is the direct opposite of being cheerful. (उदास, निराश)
◦ Example: He was in a gloomy mood after failing the interview, quite unlike his usual cheerful self.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Sunny" means bright and cheerful (often used figuratively for a pleasant disposition) — this is a synonym of "cheerful", not an antonym.

• Option 2: "Hilarious" means extremely funny — this is related in tone to cheerfulness (positive emotion), not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Joyful" means feeling or expressing great happiness — this is a direct synonym of "cheerful", not an antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "cheerful": jovial, jolly, sunny, joyful, buoyant.

• Antonyms of "cheerful": gloomy, glum, morose, dejected, downcast — recognizing this pair helps avoid selecting a synonym by mistake in antonym questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the sentence.
He tried to improve the working conditions in his office.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Spoil.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "improve" means to make or become better in quality, condition, or performance. (सुधारना)

• "Spoil" means to make something worse, damage its quality, or ruin it, which is the direct opposite of "improve". (बिगाड़ना)
◦ Example: Careless handling can spoil the working conditions instead of improving them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Spatter" (छींटे डालना) means to scatter small drops of liquid over something — unrelated in meaning to "improve" or its opposite.

• Option 2: "Sprinkle" (छिड़कना) means to scatter small drops or particles — also unrelated to the sense of improvement or deterioration.

• Option 3: "Specify" (निर्दिष्ट करना) means to state something clearly and precisely — unrelated to the concept of making something better or worse.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "improve": enhance, upgrade, better, refine.

• Antonyms of "improve": worsen, deteriorate, spoil, impair — commonly tested alongside near-sounding distractor words (as with "spatter"/"sprinkle" here) that share no real semantic link.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
It was her who first saw the criminal.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. she.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the structure **"It was ________ who + verb...", the pronoun functions as the subject complement** and is also effectively the subject of the following relative clause ("who first saw the criminal").

• Rule — Subjective Case Pronoun: When a personal pronoun follows a linking verb ("It was...") and is itself followed by a relative clause acting as its subject, formal/standard English requires the subjective case pronoun (I, he, she, we, they), not the objective case (me, him, her, us, them).

• Applying the rule: "It was her who..." is corrected to "It was she who...", since "she" (not "her") must perform the action of "saw" in the relative clause.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "them" is incorrect; it is a plural objective pronoun and does not agree with the singular sense intended, nor is it in the correct case.

• Option 3: "hers" is incorrect; it is a possessive pronoun (meaning "belonging to her") and cannot function as the subject of "who first saw the criminal".

• Option 4: "him" is incorrect; it is likewise an objective-case pronoun and also changes the gender, so it does not correct the case error correctly here.

NOTE

• Common "It is/was + subjective pronoun + who/that" structures tested in SSC: It is I who am responsible, It was he who called, It is they who decide.

• In casual/spoken English "It was her" is common, but SSC grammar questions test the formal, prescriptively correct subjective-case rule.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Can I please request you all to stand up?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. plead.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "request" means to politely or formally ask for something. (विनती करना, अनुरोध करना)

• "Plead" means to make an earnest, heartfelt appeal or request to someone, which shares the core sense of politely/earnestly asking someone to do something. (गुज़ारिश करना)
◦ Example: She pleaded with the committee to reconsider its decision — much like one would politely request an audience to stand up.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "require" (आवश्यकता होना) means to need something or to make something compulsory — it carries a sense of necessity or demand, which is stronger and different from a polite request.

• Option 3: "claim" (दावा करना) means to assert that something is true or to demand something as a right — it does not carry the sense of politely asking someone to do something.

• Option 4: "petition" (याचिका देना) usually refers to making a formal, often written, appeal to an authority, typically used in legal or official contexts — a narrower sense than the everyday act of politely asking an audience to stand.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "request": appeal, ask, solicit, entreat, plead.

• "Plead" and "request" are grouped together as synonyms in standard English thesauruses under the broader sense of "to ask for something wanted", which is the basis for this answer.

question:
Read the sentence carefully and select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined part.
Greta Thunberg’s tirade against environmental degeneration shocked the world leaders.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. long and angry speech.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "tirade" means a long, angry, or critical speech, typically a forceful verbal attack or denunciation. (लंबा और तीखा भाषण/आलोचना)
◦ Example: The coach launched into a tirade against the referee's decision.

• "Long and angry speech" directly captures this meaning, fitting the context of Greta Thunberg's forceful, critical address about environmental degeneration.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "minute observation" (सूक्ष्म अवलोकन) means a very small, detailed remark or note — this describes something precise and small-scale, not a long, forceful speech.

• Option 2: "debatable account" means a version of events that is open to question or dispute — this does not capture the anger or length implied by "tirade".

• Option 4: "innate liberal opinion" means a naturally-held, progressive viewpoint — this describes a type of belief, not a forceful spoken denunciation.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "tirade": diatribe, harangue, rant, invective.

• "Tirade" is frequently tested alongside similar "forceful speech" vocabulary in SSC exams: harangue (a lengthy, aggressive lecture), diatribe (a forceful verbal attack), rant (a long, passionate speech), polemic (a strong verbal/written attack on a specific view).
